posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
I was curious why those high power DPSS that only have linewidths of .1nm cannot be made to have longer coherence lengths. I looked at Sam page and saw an illustration of a DPSS laser and it seems to have a large enough oscillator to squeeze in an etalon. It the cavity non accessible on DPSS lasers?

Then I did a little digging and found a bunch of links concerning narrowing the linewidth of lasers with an external cavity.

[http://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/e ... 261t.alice](http://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/els/00304018/2003/00000218/00000001/art01175;jsessionid=108rdfsef261t.alice)

But all the papers are for sale. Does anyone know of this process?

I guess it would be very advantageous for holographers if we could find a way to use those very inexpensive DPSS green lasers found on E-bay for very cheap but only have a linewidth of .1nm.

Any thoughts or discussions?

posts.author: Ron Michael
posts.content_md:
Besides etalon, 

GJ Friel, AJ Kemp, K. Lake, BD Sinclair, "Compact and efficient Nd:YVO4 laser that generates a tunable single frequency green output" was a paper that generated over 200mw of slm output using a bk7 Brewster plate and KTP crystal to form a birefringent filter. I think their resonator length was 15mm.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md: The problems with some of the cheap DPSS lasers is that they use a hybrid crystal. These are crystals where the nd:YVO4 crystal is glued to the KTP crystal. The facets of the crystals are coated like mirrors. So, if you have a laser where the crystals are separated and the mirrors are not the facets of the crystals, I guess it should be fairly easy.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Thanks Hans. I wonder if the joined crystals can be removed and or separated, put on gimbals, then an intracavity etalon put in.

Those cheap DPSS lasers are in the watts for very little money and giving up a portion to the etalon may still prove cost efficient.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
> **JohnFP:** Thanks Hans. I wonder if the joined crystals can be removed and or separated, put on gimbals, then an intracavity etalon put in.

Nope, even thermal stresses can make the glue do funny things at the interface. The alt.laser guys talk often about this.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md: At [http://www.casix.com/product/Laser_DPSS.htm](http://www.casix.com/product/Laser_DPSS.htm) they sell kits for making your own DPSS lasers. With one of those kits it should not be so difficult to insert your own etalon. But I think it should also be possible to use the KTP crystal as an etalon, provided that it's temperature is properly controlled.

posts.author: Ron Michael
posts.content_md:
Unless you can get etalons cheap... they are generally expensive as they require high precision figure of lambda/10 and 10/5 scratch/dig and require parallelism of a few arc seconds not arc minutes or degrees. 

Additionally high reflectivity is needed to give a high finese inorder to effectively mode select. Likewise Fabry perot resonators make good discriminators for observing modes in lasers

No comment on the paper I gave and it's technique so I assume you guys already have read it, but it is a cheap way of making a slm tem00 laser using just a few cheap parts available from vendors like casix and a cheap bk7 plate plus a moderate expensive 1.2W fiber coupled diode pump and collimator. Depending on your technique even that can be done away with a well focused free space propagated diode pump. The point of papers like that is if you take advantage of short resonators and microchip parts and some simple but effective gain modulation techniques as they and you have suggested, it's easy to get to slm mode lasers.

Sometimes if you do a Google search on various combinations of the author name and keywords from the paper you can find a free preprint pdf out there, usually on the author's academic web page. Since scientific reputation is based on how frequently their work is cited, scientists often assert the right to freely distribute their papers personally rather than see them forever locked up as the property of the obscure journals that they were obliged to publish in.
